utterances.text: Your Honour, we would seek to tender those two documents at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 1D160 will become Exhibit 1D42, Your Honours, and document 1D161 will become Exhibit 1D43, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, there is another area of your evidence that I would like to discuss briefly with you. I think you've -- you've given some evidence about special units. Do you recall that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I think you've indicated in your statement that on one or a number of occasion, you took part in operations with the special police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subsequent to these events, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can you recall the date of that or this event? Was it -- first, was it one occasion, was it two occasions?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a number of occasions; it was more than two.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You've indicated it was either of the events that we are most interested in. Can you remember the time-period when that was?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of events in which special units were involved, and I believe the first one was probably in 2002 or early 2003 and then subsequently in 2005 and 2006. 2005, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And could you tell me which unit, which special unit or special police unit you operated with on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think "operated with" is too strong. I was present at operations in which they were involved. The -- that was the Tigers.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can you remember who the commander of the unit at the time was?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, off the top of my head, I can't. But I was aware that the commander of the unit wasn't necessarily there during those particular operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can you remember where you went observing those units?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: One occasion was near the village of Blace and another occasion was in the -- again, I can't remember the name of the village but near to the town of Gostivar -- yeah, I need to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can you explain what role exactly you played with these units as they were operating? Were you just going along with them?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I was -- in one case I had been asked to attend the scenes of an arms cache that was found at which the area was secured by the Tigers. On another occasion -- so I was there in a monitoring role. Another occasion, there was an arrest operation, a search and arrest operation underway which I accompanied, again to observe it, in my capacity as a UK advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Would you take part in the debriefings well?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did take part in the debriefings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: On every occasion or ...

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not every occasion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I think you've indicated in your statement that it was your understanding that Mr. Boskoski had the authority to give orders for -- to the Tigers unit to go into a certain location; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And so that we understand your evidence properly, sir, you're not suggesting that Mr. Boskoski was the only person who was able to give such orders?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will perhaps show you a document at this stage. It is under tab 73 which is 1D001723. It's a document signed by Mr. Goran Stravkovski, it's dated the 19th of July, 2001, and it refers to the special task unit, which was at the time the expression used for the Tigers. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And it says the following: "We notify you that with the act SD number 231-493-1 of 10 February 1999 the ESZ, special tasks unit is directly leads and commanded by the Ministry of Interior affairs, and that means that the commander of the unit receives order and task directly from the minister. Because the minister has assigned certain authority to the head of the department for police, the commander of the ESZ receive orders and tasks also from the head." So you would agree that it, in fact, is consistent with your evidence?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You've indicated as well in your statement, sir, as I understand, that you understood that it would be usual for special units such as the Tiger to prepare a plan of action before going into operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no direct knowledge of the internal planning mechanism of those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But that was your understanding or at least the understanding that you related to the Prosecution, that it would be usual to have such a plan drawn up?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And it would also be usual, wouldn't it, for the special unit in question to be registering in its log-book the fact that they were operating in a particular area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they maintained a log-book. I have no knowledge as to whether or not a log-book was maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Fair enough. There is one more paragraph, sir, which I would like to ask to you look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But before I do that, Your Honour, I will seek to tender the previous document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, it's --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D44, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, I will ask you once again to look at the statement of Mr. Zafirovski which I hope you still have in front of you. It's under tab 70.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can I ask you to turn to page 2, sir, and it would be paragraph 9 of that statement. It relates to the involvement of the special unit. And Mr. Zafirovski says this: "The involvement of the special unit is connected to the respecting of the procedures which involved that there is a need for a plan to be made for their intervention. There should a formal written decision about it. Also, the intervention of that unit should be registered in the unit's diary." I think your evidence, sir, is that you don't know about those procedures, and I don't want to put to you things that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I have no knowledge of these procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The usage of the special units such as Tigers should not be confused with the usage of the special unit of the police. Sir, at the time, were you aware of the difference between special unit and what was referred to as posebna?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- not at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And he goes on further down in the paragraph to say this then: "The procedure for activating of the special unit," -- well, I think I will skip that question, sir, if you don't know what the posebna is.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage the cross-examination would be tentatively finished and terminated with the caveat that was mentioned before about the calling of Mr. Tucker as a witness. And I don't know if Your Honour want to deal with this matter at this stage or if it's more convenient that we deal with it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will see if Mr. Saxon is in a position to add anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. I had -- the Prosecution actually had sent an e-mail a short time ago to the Boskoski team and the Prosecution will keep Mr. Tucker on its list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, we're grateful for the indication and grateful to Mr. Bolton for his patience. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. Thank you. Mr. Apostolski, is it convenient for you to proceed in the -- what remains until a quarter to two?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in agreement with Mr. Boskoski Defence, I will not be asking any questions, so I think that my colleague, Mr. Mettraux, who was quite thoroughly -- the witness was thoroughly examined. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Apostolski. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, my colleague asked you a few questions about the -- your activities on the 14th of August, 2001. And he asked you -- you explained of course that you wanted an investigative judge to come to the village that day. But -- and you were trying to make that happen through what you refer to as the command element of the Skopje police. Why was it important to speak to the command element, as you termed it? Why couldn't you just speak to the commander of Mirkovci police station, for example?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time we had very little communication or contact with the police. Prior to my arrival in Macedonia, the communication had been -- or most of the liaison and communication had taken place between the mission headquarters and the Ministry of Interior. Once we established, if you like, regional areas of responsibility within the OSCE, we then had to -- we then had to -- we then as I'd mentioned earlier, try and develop a working relationship with the regional police command at the SVR level. So at that time whilst we were aware of contact within the SVR at the regional level, we didn't have contacts at the police station level. I was aware of colleagues of mine who had met with police station commanders, but I didn't have telephone numbers for them; and I didn't have personal knowledge of them at that stage. But maybe one two, but not -- not for that area. Therefore, we approached the only point of contact that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could please, and if I could the assistance of the court officer, could we see displayed Exhibit P239. I'm wondering if we could zoom in a little bit more on this photograph, please. Thank you. I believe it was yesterday when you told my colleague that you were not able to judge the distances from which particular deceased persons had been shot. And I'm referring to, obviously, the bodies that you saw on the 14th of August. But I'd like to direct your attention to this photograph and this particular body, and I'm wondering perhaps if we could zoom in a little bit more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps in fairness to the witness, I think the question was asking in relation to the three other bodies, Your Honour. Those were the bodies which were found further up in the village north. I don't think the question was asked in relation to this particular witness. If I'm wrong, I would be standing corrected, but my recollection is it is related to the other witness. If Mr. Saxon could direct us to the relevant page of the transcript, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One moment, please. Well, I suppose it may be a question of interpretation. I'm looking at what is, I believe to be, page 93 of the transcript from yesterday, and Mr. Mettraux began asking the witness. At first he talked about the first two bodies which the witness observed and the witness said: "I was concerned at the manner in which they appeared to have met their death," and then later on the witness mentions that "There were two -- two were along or near the road where it passed through a residential area. Three others were found in a field or a hill immediately above the uppermost house at the edge of town." And then the question was: "Based on the observations of the scene, including the conditions of the bodies and the wound they received, there is a particular concern regarding the circumstances of the deaths of the two men found within the town." I see now. And both of these individuals may have been shot at close range, and there were numerous spent shell casings in the area of the bodies. And my colleague asked: "Is that consistent with your own observations, sir." The witness answered "yes." And then it continues on the next page without a specific reference to the other three bodies. However, the witness does say: "I have no means to judge the distance from which they were shot or from which the bullets hit them were fired." So in the Prosecution's mind there is still some ambiguity here, and I would seek leave to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, certainly clarify that. I think the witness appeared to be making a distinction between two bodies on the one hand and the three on the other. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With respect to the two bodies on the road, with respect to the first body you see in this photograph, were you able to make any judgement about the distance from which this person received bullet wounds?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that position, you can only see a limited distance, which for me provides a maximum range from which the rounds that hit that individual could have been fired from. And in this case a bullet is a direct fire weapon. So line of sight is generally required in order to hit your target. And I would put the maximum range that that could occur from at probably some 100 metres maximum. However, I would also say that from the blood that you see there, the impact that caused some of that blood to be there that is spread across the road to the bottom left-hand corner of the photograph as we see it, would have in my judgement, in my opinion, and based on my experience with gunshot injuries would be -- it would have to be a close range shot with the body on or close to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, later on there was some discussion between my colleague and you regarding a shotgun?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That you saw in the basement of a house. And actually I need you to -- I need to ask you to actually complete a sentence that was not completely, I believe, picked up in the record. And this is from yesterday's transcript at page 103, starting around line 12. And you began to describe the practical use of a shotgun, and this is what came out in the transcript: "The practical use of such a weapon compared to a rifle which has a higher velocity bullet ..." And then you said something else which was not picked up in the record, and I'm wondering if you can complete what -- the thought you were expressing at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm really sorry to interrupt again, but the problem may be with the transcript and not with the evidence of the witness. We have the official version of the transcript, and the sentence appears to be complete. The record that Mr. Saxon is using is apparently the informal, if you want, the version that we receive from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Then I will move on. I will move on then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My colleague earlier on showed you a document that had been signed by the public prosecutor; I believe it was from the beginning of 2002. It was 1D37. And where the public prosecutor, Mr. Zivko, emphasised that the authorities had not been able to undertake an effective investigation. And I know you've been trained as a police officer, Mr. Bolton. When you were trained as a police officer to investigate possible crimes, were you trained to speak to persons who might have witnessed the events that might have been criminal act?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. It's a major -- an extremely major part of British police training, to interview witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And within the scope of witnesses in this context, would that include any police officers who might have been present when the events occurred?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you consider that an investigation that did not include such interviews with present police officers, would you consider that such an investigation would be competent and complete?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think this is a question that is proper for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it is a proper question. If something further isn't asked, the Chamber will about the implication of it. But we'll allow the question at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would feel that the investigation was certainly incomplete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the Chamber's further question is: Are you speaking of an investigation under the British system or an investigation under the system that was in force in Macedonia at the time, bearing in mind the role of an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in terms of police interviewing a witness in this way, I would be applying it to the UK system. However, my view is that any investigation that was undertaken in Macedonia at that time, in which the investigating judge did not themselves undertake those interviews with police witnesses, would also be incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I have a follow-up question on this point, Your Honour. I know the hour is late. This will be my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, let me give you a hypothetical related to Macedonia in 2001. Suppose hypothetically that the Ministry of the Interior initiated a commission or a committee to investigate the possibility that a crime had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we have to object. I really am sorry to object at every turn here, but I think the Prosecutor has to establish a basis whether Mr. Bolton knows of any such commission, knows of the role of any such commission. When shown the document signed by Mr. Mitevski, he indicated he was not aware of that request, thereby suggesting that he was not aware of the existence of the commission in question. That was the reason for us not to ask him any further question in that regard. Furthermore, the question is completely hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, hypothetical questions were certainly asked by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, there is substance in the proposition of Mr. Mettraux that you will need to establish some further foundation, and that gives rise to an issue of time, and that is there simply isn't time for you to do it now. Would you want the evidence to continue at a later time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I will -- I will withdraw the question at this point then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure that Mr. Bolton will be grateful to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then I have no further questions right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Bolton, you will be aware from the effect of that exchange that the questioning by all counsel and the Chamber is at an end. We would thank you for your attendance in The Hague and for the assistance that you have been able to give to the Chamber, and you are of course now able to return to your other interests and activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must now adjourn, already running a little late, and we resume on Monday. It's in the morning at 9.00, I'm assured.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very sorry to interrupt. Would there be any leeway from the Chamber after the witness leaves the room to spend a few moments on some procedural issues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The word is not too long are in my ear. Mr. Bolton, thank you very much. You can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The court officer will escort you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution and the Defence have a joint application to make to the Trial Chamber, and we are making this joint application after consulting with our very capable court officer, and it is an application that I will try to describe concisely and clearly. If I don't, the agreement I have with Defence counsel is they will correct me very quickly. It simply is in regard to the so-called court files that were recently admitted by the Trial Chamber from the bar table, and those would be Exhibits P46 through P55. And the issue is simply this: The Defence and the Prosecution wish to make a joint application to the Chamber for permission that these particular exhibits be renumbered. The basis for our application is that when the Trial Chamber admitted these exhibits, they were admitted under a single number, and both the Defence and the Prosecution are concerned that, in the future, particularly perhaps at the 98 bis stage and closing argument stage, when both parties and perhaps the Chamber and their staff need to refer to particular documents within these rather voluminous court files, it will be -- they will be very difficult to find as a single number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I think I can cut you short. The Chamber would certainly be of the mind that if both Prosecution and Defence can agree on a structure in which that -- a large document, such as the court file, is conveniently broken up into separate components for the purposes of becoming an exhibit, that the Chamber would be entirely prepared to follow that breakup and have the numbering of the exhibit follow that breakup.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Does the Chamber at this time wish to see a model that has been devised for such a breakup, or can we simply advise the Chamber at a later date of the work that has been done? Which would you prefer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would suggest that once you have reached agreement it be made available so that it can be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, certainly agree [indiscernible] on the overall structure. And if I could ask the usher's permission, if I could simply pass these up to the Chamber, they would give the Chamber an idea of what the parties are proposing to do with the Chamber's permission. And the reason I'm taking extra time from the Court today is that does -- this will involve a fair amount of work by the Prosecution team, and the Prosecution would simply -- would prefer to provide this sooner -- would prefer to begin this work sooner rather than later. And the document in front of you just gives you the general idea of how we will break down the individual documents contained within these court files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is not in a position to comment on the individual breaking down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And nor do we think that there would be reason for us to do so, if all parties are in agreement that the breakdown is one that is practical and will suit the needs of the trial. So the idea, in principle, appears to the Chamber to be an excellent one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any other urgent matter or is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Not for the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We, therefore, adjourn. And we resume on Monday at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of June, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
